abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Gliomas, characterized by their robust immunosuppressive microenvironment, pose a significant challenge to the efficacy of immunotherapies. The cGas/STING signaling pathway is emerging as a promising target for cancer immunotherapy. The inhibition of ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1), a pivotal regulator within cGas/STING signaling pathway, has been shown to enhance the activation cGas/STING. We investigated the impact of macrophage-specific ARF1 suppression on the phenotype of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and the subsequent tumor specific immune response. Our findings reveal that targeted downregulation of ARF1 in TAMs substantially amplifies the immune response induced by oncolytic adenoviruses, effectively reprograms these macrophages, and bolsters anti-tumor immunity. The use of oncolytic adenoviruses armed with ARF1 knockdown elements has been demonstrated to exert a significant suppressive effect on glioma growth through the concerted action of multiple pathways and effectively elicit immune memory, thereby enhancing the survival rates of tumor bearing mice and preventing tumor recurrence.

list-item.p: ARF1 suppression enhances cGas/STING activation induced by oncolytic adenovirus infection
ARF1 ablation in glioma bolsters adenovirus induced growth inhibition
Specific suppression of ARF1 in TAMs reprograms them into a pro-inflammatory state
Oncolytic adenovirus with ARF1 knockdown triggers synergistic anti-tumor effects

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gliomas are primary brain tumors that originate from glial cells.1,2 They are the most prevalent tumors in the central nervous system, accounting for approximately 80% of all malignant brain tumors.2 According to the new 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification, gliomas are categorized into isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma.3 Despite their prevalence, there are currently no effective treatments available for gliomas. Immunotherapy, which harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and combat cancer cells, has shown significant promise in recent years. However, clinical trials for glioma immunotherapy have been largely unsuccessful. This is likely attributed to several factors, including the impermeability of the blood-brain barrier, the presence of a potent immunosuppressive microenvironment, and the intrinsic heterogeneity of gliomas.4,5,6,7,8,9,10

In gliomas, the microenvironment is predominantly populated by macrophages and microglia, known collectively as tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). These cells, which have been domesticated by the tumor over time, often exist in an immunosuppressive state. Rather than inhibiting tumor growth, they may actually facilitate it, making the reprogramming of TAMs a crucial step in enhancing the effectiveness of glioma immunotherapy.4,11,12

The cGas/STING signaling pathway plays a crucial role in the innate immune response. By recognizing exogenous (e.g., virus DNA) or endogenous (e.g., mitochondrial DNA [mtDNA]) double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) molecules, cGas induces the activation of downstream STING signaling, thereby triggering the release of type I interferons.13 Intratumoral injection of STING agonists has been shown to activate STING signaling within the tumor microenvironment (TME) and effectively suppress glioma growth.14,15,16 ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1), a GTPase belonging to the ARFs family,17 is a key regulator of the cGas/STING pathway. It can modulate this pathway in two ways: by promoting mitochondrial dynamics to prevent the aberrant release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), thus reducing cGas/STING activation; and by mediating the retrograde transport of activated STING from the Golgi apparatus, thereby inhibiting the pathway.18 Given that adenoviruses are natural activators of the cGas/STING signaling,19,20 it is hypothesized that reducing ARF1 expression in TAMs during oncolytic virus-based immunotherapy could significantly enhance the innate antiviral immune response. This approach could reprogram TAMs and alter the immunosuppressive glioma microenvironment. At the same time, a large number of tumor antigens released in the TME due to the lysis of tumor cells by oncolytic virus can be phagocytized by reprogrammed TAMs,21 which may result in improved tumor antigen presentation and induce stronger tumor antigen-specific immune responses. Here, through in vitro and in vivo experiments, we validate the possibility of intratumoral injection of oncolytic adenovirus carrying a TAMs specific ARF1 knockdown element in reprogramming TME, inducing tumor specific immune response, and subsequently suppressing the development and recurrence of glioma.

sec.title: ARF1 knockout enhances adenovirus induced activation of macrophage
sec.p:
The cGas/STING signaling pathway, known for its response to dsDNA, is a key player in the innate immune response.18 Since adenovirus is a nature activator of cGas/STING, our investigation aimed to ascertain whether the absence of ARF1 could intensify STING activation in cells infected with adenovirus. First, bone-marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) was isolated from Cas9 transgenic mice and differentiated in vitro. Utilizing the CRISPR-Cas9 system, we effectively knocked out ARF1 in primary macrophages (Figure 1A). Then these ARF1 KO macrophage and control cells were infected with D24 oncolytic adenovirus (Figure 1B), the expression of STING downstream molecules was analyzed by reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) (Figure 1C) and ELISA (Figure 1D). Our findings revealed a significant boost in cGas/STING signaling and type I interferon secretion upon ARF1 knockout, suggesting a heightened immune response. Furthermore, enhanced MHC-II expression indicates an improved antigen presentation ability of macrophage after ARF1 knockout (Figure 1E). Conditional mediums from the above ARF1 KO macrophage or control cells were collected and used to culture GL261 cell line to analyze their toxicity to glioma. As shown in the result, ARF1 KO macrophage displays enhanced suppression to the growth of glioma (Figure 1F), while inhibition of STING signaling in macrophage abolishes this effect (Figure S1). These results indicate that ARF1 knockout in macrophage enhances the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines which probably exerts a direct inhibitory effect on the growth of gliomas.Figure 1
ARF1 knockout enhances macrophage activation
Monocytes were isolated from the bone marrow Cas9 mice and cultured in vitro to differentiate into primary macrophages. Cells were then infected by lentivirus carrying an sgARF1 expression cassette and selected by 2 μg/mL puromycin for 3 days to build ARF1 knockout primary macrophage.
(A) Knockout of ARF1 was confirmed by RT-PCR. RNA from sgARF1 or sgScram treated macrophage was extracted and the expression of ARF1 was analyzed by real-time PCR.
(B) Oncolytic adenovirus infects primary macrophage with high efficiency. ARF1 KO or control macrophage seeded in 24-well plate was infected by 50 MOI adenovirus, 48 h later, cells were examined under a fluorescence microscope. Scale bars: 200 μm.
(C–F) ARF1 knockout enhances cGas/STING signaling activation. Oncolytic adenovirus infected ARF1 KO macrophages or control cells were lysed by Trizol to extract RNA. (C and D) The expression of inflammatory molecules was detected by RT-PCR (C) and ELISA (D). (E) The expression of MHC-II was elevated after ARF1 knockout. (F) ARF1 knockout polarizes macrophage into M1 state. ARF1 knockout or control macrophage was infected by oncolytic adenovirus, and the expression of M1 or M2 marker genes was analysis by RT-PCR 48 h after infection.
(G) ARF1 KO increases the toxicity of macrophage to glioma. The supernatants from oncolytic adenovirus infected ARF1 KO macrophages or control cells were collected 48 h after infection and used to culture GL261 cell line in vitro, cells were collected at indicated time points and analyzed by CCK8 assay.
(H) The enhancement of macrophage activation due to ARF1 knockout was abrogated by STING inhibition. ARF1 KO macrophages or control cells were pre-treated with STING inhibitor C-176, and followed by infection with oncolytic adenovirus, the expression of inflammatory molecules was analyzed by RT-PCR. All results are presented as means ± SD.

To elucidate whether the intensified inflammatory response in ARF1-deficient macrophages is solely mediated through the STING signaling pathway or involves additional pathways, we further investigated the immune response to viral infection in ARF1 knockout cells and control cells with the STING signal inhibited. The outcomes revealed that upon STING signaling inhibition, no significant disparity in the expression of inflammatory genes was observed between ARF1-deficient cells and control cells following viral infection (Figure 1G). This result was also confirmed in STING KO cells (Figure S2). This suggests that the absence of ARF1 in macrophages intensifies the cGas/STING signaling cascade upon viral infection, thereby propelling macrophages toward a proinflammatory state.

sec.title: ARF1 inhibition in tumor cells further enhances macrophage activation
sec.p:
ARF1 expression within tumor cells also plays important role in tumor development and tumor immune escape.22,23 Therefore, we further verified whether the oncolytic adenovirus carrying an ARF1 knockdown element could suppress the growth of glioma and further augment macrophage activation upon infecting glioma cells. As expected, infection with Ad-D24 markedly suppressed the proliferation of glioma cells, which may be mainly due to the amplification of the oncolytic virus within the cells, thereby suppressing glioma proliferation (Figure 2A). Concurrently, Ad-D24 infection also triggered the upregulation of certain inflammation-associated molecules within glioma cells (Figure 2B). However, upon ARF1 knockout (Figure 2C), the expression of these inflammation-associated molecules within tumor cells was substantially elevated (Figure 2D), and the suppressive effect on cell proliferation became even more pronounced (Figure 2E). Then the supernatants from cultured glioma cells were utilized to cultivate primary macrophages, revealing that glioma cells with ARF1 ablation could more potently activate macrophages compared to the control (Figure 2F). Existing studies have shown that ARF1 ablation in tumor cells can enhance immune response through diverse signaling pathways, and our results also confirm this. In addition, the absence of ARF1 in tumor cells can also directly impede tumor proliferation. The infection of oncolytic viruses can cause the lysis of tumor cells. Therefore, the infection of tumor cells with oncolytic viruses carrying the ARF1 knockdown element can exert a synergistic effect through multiple pathways to suppress tumor progression. Studies have indicated that the activation of STING signaling can affect viral replication.24 Consequently, we examined whether ARF1 knockout in glioma cells would impact the replication capacity of oncolytic viruses within tumor cells, which may suppress the lysis of tumor cells and the release of tumor antigens. The results showed no significant difference (Figure 2G), which is consistent with previous studies.25,26 In conclusion, inhibiting ARF1 not only enhances STING signaling in glioma cells but also further boosts macrophage activation. However, the expression patterns of some downstream genes in the STING signaling pathway after ARF1 knockout differ between glioma cells and macrophages, which may reflect the distinct responses of glioma cells and macrophages to STING activation and oncolytic adenovirus infection.Figure 2

sec.title: TAMs-specific inhibition of ARF1 improves tumor cytotoxicity of oncolytic adenovirus
sec.p:
Gliomas are characterized by a highly immunosuppressive microenvironment, which has been a major impediment to the efficacy of current clinical immunotherapies.11 Unlike other tumors, the immune cell population in glioma microenvironment is dominated by macrophages and microglia, which are predominantly in an anti-inflammatory state, significantly contributing to the immunosuppression.12 The reprogramming of these macrophages to adopt pro-inflammatory and anti-tumor properties is essential for the success of immunotherapy. Encouraged by our promising in vitro findings, we extended our investigation to assess whether the intratumoral administration of an oncolytic virus carrying TAMs-specific ARF1 knockdown elements could reprogram macrophages and effectively suppress glioma growth in mice bearing tumors. We first compared the expression of ARF1 between TAMs and macrophage/microglia in brain of naive mice; the results indicate that ARF1 expression is increased in TAMs (Figure S3). For TAMs-specific suppression of ARF1 in vivo, we engineered an oncolytic adenovirus carrying an ARF1 knockdown element under the control of a macrophage-specific promoter (Figure 3A). Upon in vitro infection of the macrophage cell line RAW264.7 with this virus, ARF1 expression was significantly diminished (Figure 3B), while ARF1 expression in glioma cells was not significantly affected (Figure S4). Consistent with the results observed in ARF1 knockout macrophages, RAW264.7 cells infected with virus carrying ARF1 knockdown element exhibited heightened activation (Figure 3C). We established a glioma-bearing mouse model by intracerebral injection of GL261-OVA cells into immunocompetent mice. Following intratumoral injection of the virus, we monitored tumor growth using an in vivo imaging system. The data revealed that while Ad-D24 injection exerted some inhibitory effect on tumor growth, it was markedly less than that of the oncolytic virus carrying TAMs-specific ARF1 knockdown element (Figures 3D and 3E). A similar trend was also observed in the mouse survival rate experiment (Figure 3F). These results reflect that ARF1 inhibition in TAMs enhances oncolytic virus-based tumor therapy. Further analysis of infiltrated immune cells in the tumor demonstrated a notable increase in immune cell numbers after Ad-D24 injection, and this increase was further amplified following ARF1 inhibition (Figure 3G). Histological assessments confirmed efficient infection of TAMs by the oncolytic virus (Figure 3H), and ex vivo analysis of sorted virus-infected TAMs revealed that inhibition of ARF1 expression promoted the transition of TAMs toward a pro-inflammatory state (Figure 3I). Moreover, TAMs-specific inhibition of ARF1 also increased the number of CD8 T cells within the tumor (Figure 3J), suggesting an enhanced antigen-specific immune response. This was further verified by in vitro experiment. After isolating tumor infiltrating CD8 T cells and performing ex vivo tumor antigen stimulation assays, we observed a significant enhancement of immune response to tumor-specific antigens in the ARF1 inhibition group (Figure 3K). Collectively, these results demonstrate that the specific inhibition of ARF1 expression in TAMs in vivo induces a pro-inflammatory shift in TAMs and bolsters the antigen-specific immune response against the tumor.Figure 3

sec.title: ARF1 inhibition enhances oncolytic virus-based immunotherapy in different glioma models
sec.p:
To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the impact of ARF1 inhibition in glioma treatment, we advanced our research by constructing an oncolytic virus equipped with an ARF1 knockdown element under the control of a EF1a promoter (Figure 4A). This design enables the suppression of ARF1 expression in both TAMs and tumor cells upon intratumoral injection, thereby allowing us to explore the therapeutic potential of the oncolytic virus with ARF1 knockdown in glioma under a multifaceted anti-tumor effect. First, this was verified in GL261 glioma model. GL261 cells were inoculated into the brains of immunocompetent mice. Then indicated viruses were intratumorally injected 7 days post tumor cells inoculation. The extension of ARF1 inhibition to tumor cells further potentiated the suppressive effect on tumor growth and significantly improved the survival rates of the tumor-bearing mice (Figures 4B–4D). Consistent outcomes were observed in the CT2A glioma model (Figures 4E–4G). In addition, the inhibition of ARF1 expression within tumor cells also increased the infiltration of immune cells within the tumor and intensified the inflammatory response (Figure 4H). As mentioned previously, TAMs-specific knockdown of ARF1 benefits tumor antigen-specific immune responses. However, the ability to induce anti-tumor immune memory is crucial for preventing tumor recurrence. Therefore, we proceeded to investigate the influence of ARF1 inhibition on the establishment of anti-tumor memory. Mice cured of GL261 tumors by OAd-EF1a-shARF1 were re-challenged with the same tumor on the contralateral side of their brains three months post the last treatment. Tumors in the mice that had previously been cured were completely rejected, exhibiting a robust resistance to recurrence, whereas tumors in the age-matched control mice progressed rapidly (Figure 4I). These findings suggest that the convergence of oncolytic virus-based immunotherapy with ARF1 inhibition can elicit a synergistic array of anti-tumor mechanisms, culminating in substantial therapeutic benefits for glioma. Concurrently, this approach can also instigate anti-tumor immune memory, effectively curbing the resurgence of glioma.Figure 4

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Malignant glioma poses a formidable clinical challenge, with the current standard of care, which includes surgery and chemotherapy, yielding suboptimal outcomes.27 Although immunotherapy has demonstrated remarkable success in hematological malignancies, its efficacy in solid tumors, particularly malignant gliomas, has been underwhelming.28 The strong immunosuppressive microenvironment and high heterogeneity of gliomas contribute to the poor outcomes of immunotherapy.8,9,10,11 The reprogramming of the glioma microenvironment is pivotal to unlocking the potential of glioma immunotherapy. The cGas/STING pathway has been implicated in tumor immune evasion, and preclinical studies in mouse models have indicated that the administration of STING agonists directly into gliomas can lead to promising therapeutic outcomes.14,15,16 Encouraged by these findings, several drugs that target the cGas/STING pathway have advanced into clinical trials.29,30

Research has highlighted ARF1 as a pivotal molecule in the regulation of the cGas/STING signaling pathway, capable of dampening STING signaling activation through the reduction of mitochondrial DNA release or by facilitating the retrograde transport of activated STING.18 While several studies have documented that the downregulation of ARF1 expression in tumor cells can directly curtail tumor growth and stimulate immune system activation,22,23 the applicability of this effect in gliomas remains unexplored. Moreover, given the glioma microenvironment’s infiltration by immunosuppressive macrophages, their reprogramming is essential for the success of glioma immunotherapy.12 Whether the suppression of ARF1 expression in macrophages can enhance the activation of the cGas/STING signaling pathway, thereby achieving the reprogramming of macrophages, has not yet been reported. In this study, we first investigated the influence of inhibiting ARF1 expression in macrophages on their immune response through in vitro experiments. We found that ARF1 suppression in macrophages predominantly amplified the activation of the cGas/STING signaling pathway, which in turn further enhanced the activation of other inflammation-related signals. Given that exogenous or endogenous double-stranded DNA serves as a natural activator of the cGas/STING signaling,13 we employed a viral vector carrying an ARF1 knockdown element to more effectively activate the cGas/STING signaling by suppressing ARF1 expression while introducing exogenous dsDNA into cells. The in vitro results substantiated this hypothesis. We further validated the impact of TAMs-specific inhibition of ARF1 expression on the TME through an immunocompetent mouse glioma model. TAMs-specific suppression of ARF1 expression fostered the reprogramming of TAMs to a pro-inflammatory state, increasing the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors, and enhancing antigen presentation capabilities. As a result, the enhanced innate immune response induced by ARF1 knockout and oncolytic adenovirus infection will improve antigen-specific immune responses. The abundance of tumor antigens is very important for effective activation of tumor-specific immune responses. The oncolytic adenovirus used here can infect glioma cells and selectively proliferate within tumor cells, causing the lysis of tumor cells and the subsequently release of a plethora of tumor antigens.21,31 These antigens, after being engulfed by reprogrammed TAMs, are presented to lymphocytes, effectively triggering an anti-tumor immune response. In this strategy, we harnessed the direct cytotoxic effect of the oncolytic virus on glioma cells and the anti-tumor immune response caused by the reshaping of TME to act in concert, achieving effective tumor elimination. Traditional vaccines typically introduce one or more tumor antigens, along with adjuvants, to elicit an anti-tumor immune response. However, due to the high heterogeneity of tumors, the efficacy of this strategy is limited, and some tumor cells may ultimately evade immune surveillance. In this study, tumor antigens are released by the lysis of tumor cells, theoretically covering all tumor antigens, thus the elicited anti-tumor immune response is also more comprehensive, which is particularly advantageous for the highly heterogeneous nature of gliomas. It has been reported that the activation of the STING signaling pathway inhibits the replication of viruses such as HSV and accelerates their clearance.24 This could potentially suppress the direct cytotoxic effect of oncolytic viruses on tumor cells and the release of tumor antigens. However, studies have shown that adenoviruses seem to have some escape mechanisms that allow them to evade the inhibitory effects of the STING signaling pathway.25,26 This is further confirmed by our results. The stability of oncolytic viruses in macrophages with ARF1 knockout was not significantly affected, and the replication capability of oncolytic viruses in ARF1 KO glioma cells was also not significantly suppressed.

Given the significant role of ARF1 expression in tumor cells in fostering tumor growth and modulating anti-tumor immune responses, the simultaneous inhibition of ARF1 in both tumor cells and TAMs could, in theory, further enhance the anti-tumor effect. In this study, we set out to test this hypothesis. Our findings revealed that while the suppression of ARF1 expression in tumor cells exerted a more pronounced inhibitory effect on tumor growth compared to its specific inhibition in TAMs, there was no significant difference in the inflammatory responses they elicited. This observation might be attributed to the overlapping mechanisms underlying the anti-tumor immune responses triggered by ARF1 inhibition in both cell types. Once ARF1 is inhibited in macrophages, the activation of the cGas/STING signaling pathway reaches its zenith, thereby rendering any additional amplification of the immune response by ARF1 inhibition in tumor cells ineffective.

In summary, this study has meticulously verified the effect of ARF1 inhibition on reshaping the glioma microenvironment and enhancing tumor antigen-specific immune responses, elucidating the underlying mechanisms in the process (Figure 5). This investigation paves the way for a novel therapeutic strategy in the realm of glioma immunotherapy, offering a promising avenue for enhancing the efficacy of treatments against this aggressive form of cancer.Figure 5

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: GL261 murine model is the most widely used syngeneic model of glioma, but GL261 model l exhibits a high infiltration of CD8 T cells which is different from the pathological characteristics of human patients. This is a limitation of this study.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
sec.p: Eight-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were purchased and bred at the Animal Center of Wenzhou Medical University, while Cas9 mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory and also bred at the Animal Center of Wenzhou Medical University. All protocols adhered to the ethical guidelines approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Wenzhou Medical University. 293T cells and RAW264.7 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS). Cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere comprising 5% CO2 at 37°C.

sec.title: Animal experiments
sec.p: To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of different virus, 5×104 of GL261-luci, GL261-OVA-luci or CT2A-luci cells were inoculated into the right striatum of C57BL6 mice. Seven days later, tumor establishment was confirmed using IVIS Imaging System. Mice were then randomly assigned into the appropriate groups and intratumorally administrated with specified virus (5×107 plaque-forming units (PFU) in 6 μl PBS) or an equivalent volume of PBS on day 7,9 and 11 post tumor cells inoculation. The growth of tumors was monitored using an IVIS Imaging System. Mice were observed daily to monitor survival and mortality, and were humanely euthanized upon exhibiting signs of distress or significant weight loss.

In rechallenge studies, C57BL6 mice which had been previously cured of GL261-luci glioma by OAd-EF1a-shARF1 or control mice were inoculated with 5×104 of GL261-luci cells into the contralateral hemisphere. The growth of tumors was monitored using an IVIS Imaging System.
All animal experiments were performed in strict compliance with the guidelines and approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Wenzhou Medical University.

sec.title: Primary macrophages isolation and culture
sec.p: Monocytes were isolated from the hind limbs of Cas9 mice. After removing red blood cells, cells were seeded into 100mm petri dishes with the density of 5 × 106 cells per dish in RPMI 1640 with 10% FBS and 20 ng/mL macrophage-Colony Stimulating Factor (M-CSF). Medium was changed every three days. Six days later, cells were gently detached using Accutase and re-seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 5×105 cells per well. The next day, cells were ready for further experiments.

To build ARF1 or STING knockout macrophage, primary macrophage isolated from Cas9 mice were seeded in 6-well plate with at a density of 5×105 cells per well. Cells were infected with lentivirus carrying sgARF1 or sgSTING expression cassette and selected by 2 μg/mL puromycin for three days. Then cells were ready for further experiments.

To inhibit STING activity, ARF1 KO macrophage or control cells were pre-treated with 2 μM C-176 for 2 h, and then infected with oncolytic adenovirus without washing the inhibitors. Cells were harvested and analyzed by RT-PCR.

sec.title: Plasmid
sec.p: pLenti-EF1a-GFP-miRE_shRen-Puro was a gift from Florian Karreth. The EF1a promoter was replaced by CD68 promoter,32 a macrophage specific promoter, for TAMs-specific expression, the obtained plasmid was named pLenti-CD68p-GFP-miRE_shRen -Puro. shRNAs targeted to ARF1 were synthesized from BGI Genomics, and ligated into pLenti-EF1a-GFP-miRE_shRen-Puro or pLenti-CD68p-GFP-miRE_ shRen- Puro through EcoRI and XhoI.

To construct oncolytic adenovirus with ARF1 inhibition element, shRNA expression cassette driven by macrophage-specific promoter (a CD68 promoter) or EF1a promoter was digested from the above lentiviral plasmid and inserted into the E1 shuttle plasmid of adenovirus. Finally, the shRNA expression cassette was transferred into adenovirus backbone plasmid through recombination, the obtained plasmid was named pOAd-CD68p-shARF1 or pOAd-EF1a-shARF1.

LentiCRISPRv2 puro was a gift from Brett Stringer. Cas9 in LentiCRISPRv2 puro was replaced by a GFP gene, the obtained plasmid was named Lenti-sgbackbone-puro. Primers for sgRNAs targeted to ARF1 were synthesized from BGI Genomics, annealed and inserted into Lenti-sgbackbone-puro through BsmBI to get sgRNA expression plasmid. All the sequences of the primers were listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Virus production
sec.p: For lentivirus packaging, the transfer plasmid was transfected into HEK293T cells together with psPAX2 and pVSVG with the ratio of 4:3:1. The supernatant was harvested at 48 h after transfection, concentrated using PEG8000, aliquoted and stored at −80 for use.

OAd-CD68p-shARF1 and OAd-EF1a-shARF1 were amplified in A549 cells, purified by Cscl2 density gradient centrifugation, and stored at −80°C, the obtained virus were named as OAd-CD68p-shARF1 and OAd-EF1a-shARF1. The viral titer was analyzed in HEK293 cells and determined as PFU/mL.

sec.title: T7E1 assay
sec.p: sgRNA expression lentivirus were used to infect MEF-Cas9 cell line, cells were selected by 2 μg/mL puromycin for seven days. Genome DNAs were isolated and amplified through PCR, about 200–300 ng PCR products were digested with 1 μL T7 endonuclease 1 for 20 min and then detected by agarose gel electrophoresis.

sec.title: ELISA
sec.p: To evaluate the secretion of STING downstream molecules, the indicated cells were seeded in 6-well plate at a density of 5 × 105 cells per well and infected with a oncolytic adenovirus at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 50. The supernatants were collected 72 h after infection, passed through a 0.45 μm filter and analyzed using Mouse IFN-beta DuoSet ELISA Kit according to the instructions.

sec.title: Analysis of tumor infiltrated immune cells
sec.p: The hemisphere where the tumor was located was digested into single-cell suspension using collagenase IV, then immune cells were obtained through 30–70% Percoll density gradient centrifugation. The number of total immune cells in each mouse was counted. For flow cytometry analysis, cells were labeled with APC-Cy7 anti-CD8 antibody at 4°C for 20 min, then fixed by Medium A, washed by FACS buffer, resuspended in 500 μl PBS, and then analyzed by flow cytometry.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Tumor tissue was fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, dehydrated with 30% sucrose, embedded in OCT, and sectioned with a cryostat. The sections were then incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight, rinsed and then stained with the secondary antibody for 1 h. After rinsing, the sections were mounted with ProLong Gold Antifade Mountant with DAPI and observed under a fluorescence microscope.

sec.title: CCK8 assay
sec.p: To analyze the toxicity of macrophage conditional medium to tumor cells, ARF1 knockout macrophages and control cells were infected with 50 MOI of oncolytic adenovirus, supernatants were collected 48 h after infection and passed through 0.45 μm filter. GL261 cells were seeded into 96-well plate with the density of 5000 cells per well and supplied with 200 μl indicated macrophage conditional medium. Cells were harvested at different time point and analyzed using CCK-8 assay kit.

sec.title: Tumor antigen-specific CD8 T cell analysis
sec.p: Monocytes were isolated from the bone marrow of mice and differentiated into dendritic cells in vitro in RPMI1640 containing 10% FBS, 20 ng/mL GM-CSF and 20 ng/mL IL-4. At indicated time points, mice were euthanized and the hemispheres with tumors were digested into a single cell suspension with tumor dissociation kit, and then immune cells were separated through 30–70% Percoll density gradient centrifugation. Finally, CD8+ T cells were isolated using CD8a+ T Cell Isolation Kit. Dendritic cells pre-loaded with OVA peptides (100 ng/mL) for 24 h were co-cultured with tumor infiltrated CD8+ T cells at a ratio of 1:5. 48 h later, supernatants were collected and the concentrations of IFN-γ in the supernatants were analyzed using IFN-γ DuoSet Elisa Kit according to the instructions.

sec.title: TAMs reprogramming assay
sec.p: At indicated time points, mice were anesthetized and sacrificed, tumor tissues were digested into single-cell suspensions using tumor dissociation kit. Immune cells were then separated by 30–70% Percoll density gradient centrifugation, then labeled with F4/80 antibody. F4/80+GFP+ cells were sorted from total immune cells as TAMs. TAMs were lysed with Trizol to extract RNA, and the changes in the expression of inflammatory genes were detected through RT-PCR.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: GraphPad Prism 10 software was used for graphing and statistical analyses. Single comparisons were made using unpaired two-tailed t-tests. Multiple group comparisons were conducted using either one-way ANOVA (for single-factor analyses) or two-way ANOVA (for two-factor analyses). All results are presented as mean ± SD, ∗: p < 0.05, ∗∗: p < 0.01, ∗∗∗: p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗: p < 0.0001, ns indicates non-significant differences. P < 0.05 was considered significant. In vitro experiments were conducted with three independent biological replicates (n = 3). For animal studies, C57BL/6 mice were randomized into control and treatment groups (n = 5 mice per group), but survival analyses were employed larger cohort sizes (n = 8/group) to ensure statistical power. One representative of 3 experiments is shown.
